posts.title: What’s New in vcpkg (Oct 2026)
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
This blog post summarizes changes to the vcpkg package manager as part of the 2026-10-16 registry release and the 2026-09-26 tool release. These updates include configurable binary-cache compression, improved cache reliability and diagnostics, Boost 1.92, and other improvements and bug fixes.
There are now 2,877 total ports available in the vcpkg curated registry. A port is a versioned recipe for building a package from source, such as a C or C++ library.
41 new ports were added to the curated registry since the July registry release.
806 ports were updated between the July and October registry releases. As always, we validate each change to a port by building all other ports that depend on or are depended by the library that is being updated for our main triplets.
178 community contributors submitted merged PRs included in this release.
The main vcpkg repo has approximately 7,800 forks and 27,600 stars on GitHub.
vcpkg changelog (2026.10.16 release)
Tool improvements
Choose your binary-cache compression level. Use --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> or VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL to trade ZIP archive size for cache submission time. The command-line option takes precedence. Leaving both unset preserves the default compression level, and the setting does not change package ABIs or prevent restoration of existing archives. NuGet packaging is unaffected (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2125, thanks @xiaozhuai!). For example, select a lower compression level when saving ZIP-based binary-cache archives: vcpkg install --binary-cache-compression-level=1
Fixed binary cache prechecks assigning provider results to the wrong packages after filtering the action list, improving cache availability reporting (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2112, thanks @miyanyan!).
Standardized binary cache upload failure diagnostics to make cache submission problems easier to identify (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2105, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
Preserved underlying registry errors instead of replacing them with a misleading “<port> does not exist” message (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2095, thanks @bugale!).
Added the apple platform expression for port metadata, allowing one expression to cover Apple target platforms (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2121, thanks @cqundefine!).
Propagated VCPKG_SSL_REVOKE_BEST_EFFORT to spawned processes so the certificate-revocation setting applies consistently (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2098, thanks @mem16k!).
Improved Windows bootstrap proxy handling: if malformed HTTPS_PROXY or NO_PROXY settings cause an invalid parameter error, the helper warns and retries using the current user’s explicit Windows proxy settings, or a direct connection if none is configured (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2137, thanks @camillebruckmann!).
Fixed NuGet exports to include vcpkg.exe in the generated package (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2134).
Made x-add-version updates transactional so an error does not leave partially updated version metadata, while also reducing unnecessary work when processing unchanged ports (PR: Microsoft/vcpkg-tool#2050).
Notable port updates
Boost: 1.91.0 -> 1.92.0, updating the Boost collection of C++ libraries.
curl: 8.21.0#1 -> 8.23.0, updating a widely used networking library.
OpenSSL: 3.6.3 -> 3.6.5#2, refreshing the cryptography and TLS dependency.
libgit2: 1.9.4#1 -> 1.9.7, updating the Git implementation library.
Qt Base: 6.11.1#1 -> 6.11.2, updating the core Qt framework port.
Vulkan SDK components: 1.4.350.0 -> 1.4.357.0, with Vulkan headers updated from 1.4.350.1 -> 1.4.363.0.
Armadillo: 14.4.1#1 -> 15.6.1, bringing a new major version of the linear algebra library.
SDL 3: 3.4.12 -> 3.4.18, updating the cross-platform multimedia library.
22 ports were removed as part of registry maintenance: cppdap, ctp, dx, keccak-tiny, kf5diagram, libfreenect2, qtquickcontrols2, rapidfuzz, sdl1, sdl1-mixer, sdl1-net, septag-sx, shiftmedia-libgnutls, sqlpp11-connector-mysql, sqlpp11-connector-sqlite3, tensorflow, tensorflow-cc, tensorflow-common, threadpool, v8, vcpkg-tool-bazel, and vulkan-hpp.
Other minor improvements and bug fixes.
Documentation updates
The following documentation changes were published recently:
Documented VcpkgManifestInstalledBaseDir for MSBuild solutions that use manifest mode and build multiple triplets, allowing a shared installation base directory with triplet-specific subdirectories (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#588, thanks @autoantwort!).
Documented VCPKG_PROVIDED_FORTRAN, including its defaults and how custom triplets can select a different Fortran compiler (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#600).
Added documentation for vcpkg print-usage, which displays usage information for installed packages (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#599).
Documented the CURL_CA_BUNDLE environment variable for configuring the certificate authority bundle used for downloads (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#587).
Expanded the platform-expression reference with the apple and bsd platform families, additional platform identifiers, and the corrected Xbox target condition (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#612).
Documented --binary-cache-compression-level=<0-9> and VCPKG_BINARY_CACHE_COMPRESSION_LEVEL, including precedence, defaults, accepted values, and compatibility with existing cache entries (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#613, thanks @xiaozhuai!).
Clarified how a repository-level nuget.config containing <clear /> can remove inherited binary-cache sources and cause authentication failures, with guidance for keeping the authenticated source in the effective configuration (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#614, thanks @hoshiizumiya!).
Updated GitHub Actions examples to pin actions to full commit SHAs instead of version tags (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#617).
Updated the maintainer guide with a policy for AI-reported bugs in new ports: report findings upstream, accept upstream’s assessment, and close the new port submission if upstream does not respond within 30 days. The update also clarifies terminology and other maintainer guidance (PR: MicrosoftDocs/vcpkg-docs#615).

posts.title: F3 Lightning: How Meta Accelerates Ads ML Features to Production at Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Facebook Feature Framework (F3) is Meta’s framework for authoring, compiling, and serving the machine learning features underlying ads ranking models, where a single request can require more than 20,000 features. We first presented F3 at AI @ Scale 2020. 
F3 reduced execution computational costs by compiling all features into a single merged graph, but that graph also served as the release unit, so a single failure or invalid definition blocked the entire release pipeline.
This post introduces F3 Lightning, an infrastructure layer built on top of F3 to resolve this challenge by decoupling feature releases from shared execution, so each feature is compiled, validated, deployed, and rolled back independently.
The hardest part to solve was preserving F3’s efficiency improvements. Early per-feature release prototypes increased CPU usage because independent features no longer shared computation. We aimed to close this gap through four optimizations: stable computation identifiers, a single shared execution plan, one shared memory buffer across all features, and dense index mapping for direct array access.
With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than the prior F3, with no increase in infrastructure compute cost. This shorter release cycle also enables more model iterations in the same period.
A Primer on F3’s Shared Execution Architecture
Production machine learning systems rarely consume raw data directly. Before a model can make a prediction, its feature-serving system may need to read stored signals, filter events to a time window, count or sum values, normalize them, and combine intermediate results.
The simplest design to complete this work treats every feature as an independent function. That is easy to understand, but it becomes wasteful at scale, because features are not computationally independent. A seven-day click count and a seven-day impression count may read the same event source and apply the same time-window filter. A click-through rate feature may then reuse both results. Running each feature separately would repeat that filter, and every other shared step, on every request.
F3 approached this differently, by representing feature extraction as a directed acyclic graph (DAG). Each node performs one unit of work, such as reading an input, applying a filter, or calculating an aggregation. An edge means one computation depends on the result of another. The graph’s outputs are the feature values a model consumes.
Engineers author each feature independently in a high-level language. The F3 compiler turns each definition into a small graph, then merges the graphs for every feature a service uses into one merged graph (Figure 1). Where features share an operation, such as the seven-day filter above, the compiler collapses the duplicates into a single node. That shared work then runs once per request, not once for every feature that needs it. At runtime, feature extraction is a traversal of this merged graph.
Figure 1: F3 consolidates all features into one merged graph.
The Shared Graph Made Every Release All-or-Nothing
F3’s merged graph shared computation efficiently, but it came with a major catch: The graph was also the release, and one malformed definition could hold back every other feature in the merged graph.
Figure 2 illustrates this challenge. It shows seven independently authored features, A through G, where five definitions are valid, but D and G contain unrelated errors. The “Attempt 1” build fails on D, so none of the seven features ships. After D is corrected, the “Attempt 2” build reaches G and fails again. Only after both definitions are fixed in “Attempt 3” does the complete merged graph make it successfully to production.
Figure 2: One failing feature blocks the entire release.
Failures became more frequent as F3 scaled. F3 originally served a few hundred features, and at that size merges succeeded and releases were largely smooth. Today that number is more than 20,000, and different feature types need their own checks depending on how they compute, so new features and modified features are held to different testing bars. A feature that a model already consumes needs model-related tests before it can be released. Those tests are computationally expensive enough that they run only in a later release stage, and, because the merged graph ships as one unit, every other feature in it waits for them too.
F3 Lightning: Making Each Feature Its Own Release and Sharing Computation
After F3 launched, we made several rounds of improvements to the merged graph. Each one brought back release speed for a while, but the gains eroded as more features landed, because all features still shipped together in the merged graph. So F3 Lightning was built to make every feature releasable on its own while preserving F3’s efficiency. 

As illustrated in Figure 3, F3 Lightning introduced two changes to help achieve this:
Deployment granularity: Each feature is an independently releasable configuration. It is validated, shipped, and rolled back without affecting any other feature.
Efficiency parity: F3’s efficiency came from the merged graph, so giving every feature its own release removes the source of it. Matching that efficiency while keeping per-feature releases required several key optimizations in how F3 Lightning executes.
Figure 3: F3 Lightning separates the release boundary from the execution boundary.
Deployment Granularity: How F3 Lightning Isolates Feature Releases
Isolation starts in the compiler, where each feature is compiled on its own into a single configuration. That feature configuration carries everything needed to extract that feature — every node it needs, in order, with nothing borrowed from a neighbor. If feature C has a problem, feature A still ships, because the two configurations have no relationship to each other.
Figure 4: A bad feature no longer blocks a good one.
Because features are no longer merged at release time, each one can be selected and released on its own schedule. The release path becomes an ordered queue instead of a batch that ships all at once or not at all. Changes are prioritized by what they unblock. A new feature that no model consumes yet can go out quickly on standard validation, while a change to a feature a live model already reads gets extra testing first.
Figure 5: Features are selected from a priority queue by impact and risk.
Efficiency Parity: How F3 Lightning Preserved F3’s Serving Efficiency
Our first prototypes separated deployment only. Features shipped independently, but execution was no longer shared, so the prototypes used substantially more CPU than traditional F3. Each independently released configuration arrived at the serving process as its own graph and was executed separately, repeating every read, filter, and aggregation that F3’s merged graph had eliminated.
The fix was to bring shared execution back without bringing the merge back. At startup, F3 Lightning does not rebuild a merged graph. It takes the active feature configurations, consolidates the work they share, and arranges it into a single execution order. Getting back to parity took four steps: a compiler prerequisite followed by three startup optimizations.
Step 1: Stable Identifiers Make Shared Work Recognizable
To deduplicate execution, the runtime must recognize when two independently compiled configurations contain the same computation. Node numbers can’t do this, because numbering is local to each feature’s graph. The same seven-day filter might be node 2 in one configuration and node 7 in another, and inserting a single node renumbers everything after it. Traditional F3 never had this problem, because one compiler run saw every feature and could assign identifiers globally.
F3 Lightning instead has the compiler derive each identifier from what the work does, not where it sits: the operation, its parameters, and the identifiers of its inputs (see Figure 6). Because each input’s identifier already reflects everything upstream of it, the identifier captures the whole chain of work that produced the result. Where input order doesn’t affect the result, inputs are put in a standard order. Aggregations also include the properties that define their behavior, such as the time window and grouping keys. As a result, two features that define the same operation over the same inputs receive the same identifier, even if they were compiled and released weeks apart. If a computation’s meaning changes, its identifier changes with it.
Figure 6: The same computation gets the same identifier.
Step 2: One Execution Plan Across Every Feature
At service startup, F3 Lightning builds a single execution plan across all active features, using a topological sort to place every node after the nodes it depends on. When several features contain a node with the same identifier, the plan keeps one copy and connects every consumer to it, so that computation runs once no matter how many features use it.
Merging guarantees each computation runs once, but the plan is still a graph that the executor walks pointer by pointer on every request. The same startup pass therefore flattens it into an ordered list, so each request runs a single forward pass down the list instead of traversing a graph.
Sharing one plan raises a risk: A single failing computation could affect every feature. To prevent this, if a computation fails or its input is unavailable, F3 Lightning marks everything downstream of it as not ready, and the executor skips that work. A failure affects only the nodes that depend on it, and independent branches keep running.

Step 3: A Shared Memory Buffer, Because Deduplication Was Not Enough
After steps 1 and 2 were complete, no computation ran twice, yet CPU use was still above traditional F3. The remaining compute cost came from memory layout. Each configuration carried its own request-time data container, so intermediate results were scattered across separate memory allocations. Walking the plan in order meant jumping between them, and each jump cost a cache miss.
F3 Lightning replaced those per-feature containers with one buffer per request. At startup, each feature’s references are rebound to slots in that buffer. 

Three improvements follow from the single buffer:
Locality: Consecutive plan steps now touch adjacent memory, so the values a step reads are usually already in cache. This restores the sequential access pattern the merged graph always had. It also removes the per-feature allocation on every request.
One readiness vector: A single vector, stored apart from the values, replaces per-feature tracking, so the executor can check whether a value is ready without reading the value itself. The marker has to be separate because an empty list is a valid result, so “empty” can’t also mean “not computed yet.”
No duplicate copies: Most feature values are lists and maps, and consumers no longer get their own copy. The shared slot holds a reference to the producer’s result, so a computation used by 20 features is computed once and stored once. Single values (scalars) are still copied, because copying a small value is cheaper than following a pointer. This is safe because each buffer lasts only for one request, and the execution order guarantees each result outlives its last reader.
Figure 8: All features share one memory buffer.
Step 4: Dense Index Mapping Removes the Last Per-Access Cost
Values now lived together, but finding one was still computationally expensive. Every access had to resolve an identifier, which meant hashing a key, probing buckets, and following a pointer. Lookups weren’t computationally efficient at Meta’s serving volume. 
The final fix applied the same principle as steps 2 and 3, doing the work once at startup. F3 Lightning assigns every unique identifier a consecutive integer slot and rewrites every reference in every configuration to point at those slots, so identifiers are used only during initialization. Reading a result becomes a direct array index into the shared buffer, with no hashing and no lookup table on the request path.

With F3 Lightning, comparable extraction features now reach production ~3.6x faster than on traditional F3, with no increase in infrastructure computational cost. That shorter release cycle means models can be improved and retrained more often in the same period. Building F3 Lightning also taught us three lessons:
Deployment and execution should have separate boundaries: If one artifact determines both how components run and when they ship, a failure in any one of them blocks all the others. Splitting the two jobs removed a trade-off between efficiency and release speed.
Work that never changes between requests belongs at startup, not on the request path: Three tasks were identical for every request: spotting shared work, deciding the order to run it in, and finding where each result is stored. F3 Lightning now does them once, when the service starts, so independent releases add no computational cost to individual requests.
Two designs can execute the same operations in the same order and still differ substantially in CPU computational cost: In F3 Lightning, we removed every repeated computation, yet CPU use stayed above traditional F3. Each feature still kept its own copy of the shared results, spread across memory. Consolidating them into one copy per result closed the gap. This is the least obvious result in the project and the one that generalizes furthest. On modern CPUs, where results live and how many copies exist can matter as much as how many computations run.
Acknowledgments
We would like to thank Sourabh Bansal, Ping Chen, Weitao Chen, Benjamin Dummitt, Junhua Gu, Henry Hu, Jing Huo, Joffrey Liu, Rocky Liu, Weixi Ma, Shuby Mao, Sandeep Pandey, Mihir Rastogi, Tim Sombuntham, Matt Steiner, Vivienne Sung, Ritwik Tewari, Vivek Trehan, Arnaud Venet, Ziheng Wang, Gautam Wilkins, Fan Yang, Qiao Yang, Jie Zheng and the entire team behind the development and productionization of F3, Meta’s Ads ML feature computation and serving platform, and F3 Lightning, the capability built on top of it.

posts.title: Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests).
Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production.
Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests.
Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale.
Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests. More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests), a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch.
In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives.

The Advantage of Catching JiTTests
Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not.
Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests.
How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta
JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives).
It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers?
To address this, we developed two tandem workflows:
An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points.
A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”).
Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests.
To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives.
We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch.
How It Works
The entire system workflow happens in five stages:
Stage 1: Targeting and Triggering 
The system runs overnight on spare capacity and targets diffs submitted the previous day that are deemed “risky” using a mechanism similar to Diff Risk Score (DRS) and trained on previous code changes. This helps ensure test generation is focused on diffs that are most likely to contain severe regressions.
Stage 2: Two Diff-Aware Test-Generation Workflows
The dodgy diff workflow treats each diff as if it were a mutant and uses mutation-guided LLM-based test generation to produce tests that distinguish the diff’s behavior from its parent. The goal here is to maximize the pool of weak catches and with it the chances of finding a strong catch among them.
At the same time, the intent-aware workflow uses an LLM to infer the diff’s intention using the code changes, diff title, and summary. The LLM then describes the “risks”— the ways an attempt to implement the intent could produce errors. It then uses those risk descriptions to construct mutants — each representing a bug that could be introduced while implementing the inferred intent.
Tests are generated to kill each mutant (i.e., distinguish mutant behavior from parent).
Those tests are then run on the actual diff. Any that fail are harvested as weak catches.
Stage 3: LLM-as-Judge Ensemble (Automated Assessment)
Once weak catches are generated, the system must determine whether each is a false positive or actually a strong catch (true positive).
The LLM-as-Judge ensemble consists of a collection of LLMs that review:
The weak-catch test-case code.
The test-execution outcome (failure code, message, execution trace).
The code changes between parent and child (the diff).
The inferred diff intent.
Stage 4: Rule-Based Assessor (RubFake)
We complement LLM-as-Judge with a more traditional, rule-based approach called Rule-Based False-Positive Killing Environment (RubFake).
LLM-as-Judge has rich semantics, but its judgements are non-deterministic and challenging to verify. By contrast, RubFake provides verified, deterministic judgments. Working together, RubFake and LLM-as-Judge produce an overall ranking of weak-catch candidates, with those ranked sufficiently highly being worthy of further consideration.
Stage 5: Human-on-the-Loop (Engineer Reach-Out)
Based on the ranking from LLM-as-Judge and RubFake, the system then decides whether to reach out to human engineers.
Rather than a human-in-the-loop approach, where a human engineer reviews every output, we’ve reduced friction through a human-on-the-loop approach, where human engineers set criteria and review outcomes at an aggregate level rather than supervising every output.
Table 2. Operational differences between human-in-the-loop and human-on-the-loop approaches.
The Impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta
With the testing system in place, our goal is to get engineers to engage with its results.
As of this writing, 589 engineers at Meta (64% of our outreach) have engaged with Catching JiTTests. These engineers have reported that Catching JiTTests surfaces genuinely actionable findings, with a 60% rate of true positives.
In the first half of 2026, Catching JiTTests played a key role in catching 74 serious (SEV) privacy bugs at the diff stage, before they landed in production and lowering the overall occurrence of privacy SEVs by 20% during that timeframe.
Figure 2. The impact of Catching JiTTests at Meta in the first half of 2026.
Why It Matters
Agentic software development is helping engineers and developers across the industry write, review, and ship code faster than ever before. But faster deployment means there’s also a need for faster testing. Every bug caught before it reaches production is one that end users never need to deal with. We’ve shown that LLMs can provide an additional safety layer capable of catching what traditional tests may miss, demonstrating that AI-generated testing can scale enough to reduce organizational risk. 
Catching JiTTests is a solution that is scalable, both technologically and socially. Combining these tests with a human-on-the-loop approach helps ensure that engineers rarely need to read test code and only need to confirm whether an observed behavioral change was intended.
The approach is generalizable: Engineers define success criteria early, let AI execute the testing, monitor the outcomes at an aggregate level, and intervene at the policy level rather than per item.
Read the Paper
Our paper, “Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta,” which was presented at FSE 2026 and featured at Product@Scale, details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests in Meta’s infrastructure.

posts.title: How to Use AI for Rust Development: Lessons From an OpenAI Engineer
posts.content:encodedSnippet: “Some people use AI to write more code. I use AI to make my code more correct.” Predrag Gruevski’s pinned post sums up his approach to using AI for Rust development. Predrag works on frontier systems at OpenAI, and he created cargo-semver-checks and Trustfall. In his work, there’s very little room for error. Still, he does most of his engineering with AI in the loop, and his quality bar has gone up. But how? We wanted to know what that looks like in practice, so we invited him to a RustRover livestream. His presentation was part of our AI & Rust livestream series with the Rust Foundation, which looks at real-world use cases, successes, and failures where Rust and AI meet. This post focuses on Predrag’s most practical advice: what to review, how to prompt AI coding agents, how to verify their work, and what to do when they get something wrong You can watch the full livestream recording here 👇 Which Rust code deserves the most attention when you use AI? Before you hand anything to an AI agent, sort the work by how much it would cost to get wrong. Not every line of code is equally important. Some lines deserve 1000 times more attention than others. When you typed every line yourself, 10 lines of unsafe Rust and 10 lines of regular code took about the same amount of time to write. Now AI handles the regular code, so you can move that time to the lines where mistakes are expensive. Think of your code on a risk scale. At one end, a mistake is cheap to spot and fix. At the other, it can stay hidden for months and do real damage. Here are three points on that scale: Low-stakes code. A GitHub Actions workflow is a good example. You know what it should do, and the agent has read the docs, so let it write the workflow and test it. If a CI bash script breaks and nothing security-related is at stake, ask the agent to fix it. Logic that other people rely on. cargo-semver-checks catches breaking changes before they ship, and it now runs in Rust’s own CI. In the five years before it was added, it could have caught around half a dozen accidental breaking changes in Rust releases that forced backports. On the other hand, if its logic is wrong and it tells someone their change is breaking when it isn’t, that’s a very serious problem. So while preparing it for Rust’s CI, Predrag asked AI to construct standard library additions that would trigger false alarms. That scrutiny uncovered false alarms that could affect regular libraries, too. Code like this deserves much more of your time. Unsafe code. A mistake here can mean memory unsafety, security issues, or a Heisenbug that shows up one time in a billion. That sounds rare until you run it in a data center. There, corrupting data 0.0000001% of the time means it happens all the time. In one real case, a problem of this sort was caused by a mere 20 lines in an unsafe block. This is the code worth reading line by line, or even writing manually. Four hours is a fair price to spend on 100 lines of unsafe code. How do you prompt AI coding agents to write reliable Rust? Describe what you want, how you want it done, and what “good enough” means. Don’t settle for “these ten lines of code, please”. A single task can use billions of tokens, producing far more code than you’ll ever read, so the engineering has to happen in the prompt. To write a good prompt, you need to do three things: Sketch the design Brief the agent the way you’d brief a very skilled, very diligent colleague who doesn’t have your context. At a whiteboard, you’d draw some boxes and arrows. You’d explain how the types work, which functions and fields you need, and what data goes where. Those are the load-bearing bits. Put them in the prompt and let the agent expand on them. Do the same for tests. The variable names inside a test case matter much less than the test structure. Do the tests cover all the major cases? Does the right thing happen at the right point in time? Describe that structure in the prompt. Say which assumptions are acceptable If you tell a model to be thorough and test everything, you’ll get tests for a meteor strike during a power outage. For aircraft software, that’s the right level of care. For most code, it’s wasted effort. Tell the agent which assumptions are fine, and ask it to check whether a scenario could really happen. Be precise Rust questions often have conditional answers. Ask whether a particular change is breaking, and the accurate answer might be “yes, with six caveats”. It depends on whether the trait already existed, whether it was implemented on a type that already existed, whether the trait was sealed, and so on. Your prompts need the same degree of precision about what you want and what you don’t. All of this takes time, and it pays off. To look for speedups in the Rust compiler and standard library, Predrag spent 45 minutes writing one prompt for Codex. It told the agent where to look: hot code nobody had optimized in a while. It said which changes to prefer: small ones that reuse ideas that already worked elsewhere in the project. And it said how to benchmark: interleaved runs, with at least a 1% improvement in geometric mean. In one PR, Predrag deleted a single line in the new trait solver. The line recomputed something the code had already computed 40 lines earlier. Removing it made the new trait solver up to 7.5% faster. Once someone points that out, everyone agrees the line should go, but finding it took a lot of engineering and thought. “It’s very easy to think of AI as just a faster horse. This is an example of it not being a faster horse. In principle, we could have done all of this work manually. It just would have taken five years to find these optimizations.” Predrag Gruevski Software Engineer, Frontier Systems at OpenAI How do you verify AI-generated Rust code? Focus your review on the design and on how the code is tested. Once agents followed instructions reliably, reading every line no longer turned up issues for Predrag. So he moved on to higher-level questions. Is the API designed well? Are we testing it in all the right ways? Why advanced testing is suddenly practical Code coverage, branch coverage, mutation testing, and deterministic simulation were always available, but they took too much effort to use regularly. An agent that reliably follows a process changes that. Describe the process in the prompt, and the agent does the heavy lifting. A verification process you can hand to an agent Say you’re building a component with a state machine inside. Each step should catch something the previous one can miss: Test the structure. A harness that tests every state and every transition shows that each one behaves correctly. Check coverage on the logic that matters. A coverage tool shows which code the tests execute. Make sure all the non-trivial logic is included. Check that the tests catch bugs. Simply executing a line doesn’t prove that the tests check what it does. cargo-mutants intentionally introduces bugs into your code and checks whether any test catches them. Each surviving mutant is a prompt to investigate whether the tests missed an important behavior. Add test cases until the code is pinned down in all the right places. Run unsafe code under Miri and sanitizers. Have the agent think through the important cases and test them under Miri and sanitizers like ASan. These tools work alongside the careful review of the safety invariants, which still deserve your full attention. As a prompt, the process can look like this: This component has a state machine inside. The states are [...] and the transitions are [...]. Write a harness that tests every state and every transition and checks that the right thing happens. Run a coverage tool and make sure the tests execute all non-trivial logic. Panic branches on .unwrap() for illegal input don't need tests. Run cargo-mutants. For each surviving mutant, check whether the tests miss an important behavior, and add test cases where they do. For any unsafe code, think through the important cases, write tests for them, and run those tests under Miri and ASan. I'll review the safety invariants myself. What should you do when an AI agent gets it wrong? Sooner or later, an agent will hand you a result you don’t like. Approach the problem with empathy. Work out why the agent decided on the approach it took and what it would have needed to know to decide differently. If you can’t tell, ask it. Then put the answer into your setup. If the agent keeps testing unrealistic failures, like that meteor strike, add a line to your agent’s instructions file (such as AGENTS.md). Tell it to make pragmatic assumptions about real-world failures. You can also update your personalization prompt or tweak your skills. Next time, the agent should make a better call. Nobody is born good at using AI tools. Getting good can take many billions of tokens, and we’re all still learning. How do you know AI-generated code is good enough to ship? That depends on what you’re building. Vibe coding is perfectly reasonable for tasks like prototyping, where you just want to know whether an approach works at all, and it’s also fine in apps you build for yourself. If the thing that turns on your lights at 7 pm breaks, it breaks. Vibe coding is fine there. Production code needs a higher standard. Use AI to reach a level you couldn’t hit alone. To get there, work backward. Think about how you’d convince someone else that what you built is good, even someone who doesn’t know your domain. For work on the Rust compiler, proof meant a few lines of code, faster benchmarks, a passing test suite, and a change anyone can read and understand. Once you know what proof looks like, set up your workflow to produce it. Pretty quickly, you’ll realize that the person you’re convincing could be you. Every piece of code you push has your signature on it. It literally comes from your Git client. Use AI to make sure it’s code you’d be proud to put out in the world. Want more? Watch the full conversation above. For the other side of Rust and AI, read our post on building LLM applications with Rig. Is AI useful for Rust development? Yes, especially when you use it to raise your quality bar rather than only to write more code. Agents make it practical to run techniques that used to take too much effort, such as mutation testing, full state-machine coverage, and checking unsafe code under Miri. They can also dig through Git history to find hot code nobody has optimized in a while. Do you need to read every line of AI-generated Rust code? No. Match the review to the risk. For low-stakes code like a CI script, testing that it works is usually enough. Logic other people rely on deserves much more of your time, and unsafe Rust is worth reading line by line or writing by hand. Can AI coding agents write unsafe Rust? They can, but unsafe Rust needs the most care of any code you work on. Have the agent think through the important cases and test them under Miri and sanitizers like ASan, and review the safety invariants yourself.

posts.title: JetBrains Foundation to discontinue new scholarships at Constructor University starting in 2027
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
As JetBrains’ business direction evolves, we’re reviewing how our educational initiatives align with our priorities. As part of this shift, we’ve made the difficult decision to stop offering new scholarships at Constructor University.
We know this is disappointing news, especially if you were preparing to apply or have already submitted an application. We’re sorry for the uncertainty this brings to your plans.
Our commitments to current students remain unchanged. All existing Software, Data and Technology (SDT) and Advanced Software Technology (AST) scholarship recipients will retain the benefits covered by their scholarship agreements until graduation. JetBrains experts will also continue their teaching involvement in the SDT and AST programs for current scholarship students.
Our commitment to supporting talented young people through education continues. Our Math, AI, and Coding Clubs, Youth Coding and Math Challenges will continue as planned, along with the upcoming ACTS 2027.1 training camp.
We’ll also share an update on admissions and scholarship opportunities at Neapolis University Pafos on February 1, 2027.
We’re grateful to all the students, families, teachers, and coaches who have placed their trust in our programs. We understand how important clear and honest communication is, especially during times of change, and we’ll continue sharing updates as more information becomes available.
FAQ
1. Will there be any new JetBrains Foundation scholarships at Constructor University?
No. We will not offer new scholarships at Constructor University Bremen for the foreseeable future. Current scholarship students will continue receiving all the benefits in their scholarship agreements until graduation.
3. Why is JetBrains  Foundation ending these scholarships?
As JetBrains’ business direction evolves, we’re reviewing how our educational initiatives align with our priorities. As part of this shift, we’ve made the difficult decision to stop offering new scholarships at Constructor University. This decision follows a review of our educational initiatives and how they align with JetBrains’ evolving priorities.
We know this is disappointing for students who hoped to apply. Our commitments to current scholarship recipients remain unchanged, and we will continue supporting them through graduation.
Our commitment to supporting talented young people through education also continues. Our Math, AI, and Coding Clubs, Youth Coding and Math Challenges will continue as planned, along with the upcoming ACTS 2027.1 training camp.
3. I’ve already started preparing or applying. What does this mean for me?
Unfortunately, we won’t be awarding new JetBrains Foundation Scholarships at Constructor University for the 2027 intake.
We know you may have invested considerable time and effort in preparing your application, and we’re sorry if this decision affects your plans.
If you’ve already submitted an application or have questions about your individual situation, please contact Sofana Rojas Vargas from Constructor University recruiting directly: srojasvarg@constructor.university.  
4. Are there other scholarships or funding options I can apply for?
Constructor University offers various financial aid options, including scholarships for numerous degree programs. 
In the meantime, you can explore other degree programs and funding opportunities available at Constructor University here.
We’ll also share an update on scholarship opportunities at Neapolis University Pafos on February 1, 2027.
5. Can I still apply for a JetBrains Foundation scholarship at Neapolis University Pafos?
We will share an update on the next admissions round and scholarship opportunities at Neapolis University Pafos on February 1, 2027.
6. Can my application or selection results be transferred to the Pafos scholarship process?
No. Neapolis University Pafos has a separate admissions process and its requirements are different. You will need to apply separately and complete its selection process. Please reach out to us directly if you have any questions and need our support. 
7. Will current SDT students be able to finish their degrees?
Yes. Our agreement with Constructor University explicitly provides for current students to complete their studies.
All existing JetBrains Foundation scholarship recipients will also retain the full benefits covered by their scholarship agreements until graduation, including tuition, accommodation, and other covered expenses.
JetBrains will continue its academic involvement with current SDT and AST students.

posts.title: The User Group Support Program Is Becoming the Developer Communities Program
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Great developer communities don’t come together by accident – they’re built by people who consistently show up for others. They organize meetups after work, keep online discussions active, invite speakers, prepare workshops, and create spaces where developers can learn from each other.
At JetBrains, we’ve always valued these efforts and had the privilege of supporting community organizers around the world. Today, we’re taking the next step in how we do that.




Communities have changed, and so have we
When we first launched the JetBrains User Group Support Program thirteen years ago, the idea was simple. We wanted to help local developer groups grow by providing JetBrains IDE subscriptions for organizers and small community giveaways. Since then, the way developer communities work has changed greatly.
Many communities now live online, on Discord, Slack, and other platforms. Others move between in-person and virtual events, depending on what works best. Workshops, livestreams, and hybrid events have become part of everyday community life.
We realized our program should evolve together with the communities.
That’s why our User Group Support Program is becoming the JetBrains Developer Communities Program, designed to better support the many ways developers come together today.




Supporting more communities, in more ways
Our goal hasn’t changed. We still want to help communities create opportunities for developers to learn, connect, and exchange ideas. What is changing is how we support that.
The program now welcomes a much broader range of communities, including:
Online communities
Hybrid communities
Local meetup groups
Workshops and other developer-focused initiatives
We’re also expanding the types of support available. In addition to JetBrains IDE subscriptions for organizers and community giveaways, communities may also receive:
JetBrains swag
Ready-to-use content
Help connecting with speakers
Visibility through JetBrains channels
Sponsorship for selected events
Opportunities to host meetups at JetBrains offices
Every community is different, so support won’t look exactly the same for everyone. We’ll work with organizers to understand what would be most useful, based on the activities, needs, location, and available resources.
Existing User Group Support Program participants will automatically become part of the Developer Communities Program – there’s no need to reapply.
Running a student community? School, college, and university student clubs aren’t covered by this program. If you’re a student looking for free JetBrains tools, check out the JetBrains Student Pack.




Staying connected
We see this program as a long-term collaboration with community leaders. As the program grows, we want to stay closer to the communities we support.
Starting in 2027, we’ll check in with participating communities once a year to hear what they’ve been working on and how we can help going forward.
Join us
If you lead an active, established developer community, we’d like to hear from you! We look at each community individually and consider its activities, audience, and engagement.
Learn more about the JetBrains Developer Communities Program and apply today
                                                    
Thank you to everyone who puts time and energy into helping developers connect and grow!

posts.title: Use Your GitHub Copilot Plan in JetBrains Air – in Your IDE and in the Cloud
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
GitHub and JetBrains are bringing GitHub Copilot to JetBrains Air. Air lets you hand coding tasks to agents, run them in parallel, and review their changes in one place. You can now pick GitHub Copilot as the agent in Air – locally in your JetBrains IDE, and in the cloud with Air Teams. Tasks run on your existing Copilot plan, not on JetBrains AI credits.
Air runs the official GitHub Copilot CLI over the Agent Client Protocol (ACP), the open protocol Air uses to connect agents. You get the real GitHub Copilot agent and the models it offers you, in the same task list as Claude, Codex, and Junie. With Air Teams, you can hand GitHub Copilot a cloud task and close your laptop, and it’ll keep working on its own sandboxed machine.
Try it now in your JetBrains IDE or on the web.
Run GitHub Copilot locally in your IDE
GitHub Copilot runs locally in Air in JetBrains IDEs through ACP. You don’t need Air Teams, but you do need a GitHub Copilot subscription.
Install Air in your JetBrains IDE and open it.
Choose GitHub Copilot in the agent picker.
Sign in with GitHub when Air prompts you to do so.
Describe your task and click Send.
GitHub Copilot works in your local project, and you review its changes in Air as with any other agent.
How to run your first GitHub Copilot task in the cloud
With Air Teams, GitHub Copilot can also run in the cloud. You can start a cloud task from your IDE or the web, and it keeps working after you close your laptop.
What you need
A JetBrains Account with a company that uses Air Teams (available to JetBrains business customers).
A GitHub Copilot subscription.
A GitHub Copilot cloud task started from IntelliJ Idea



We recommend starting with a small, well-defined task – maybe something you’d normally put off: a flaky test, a dependency bump, or a small bug with a clear repro.
From the web
Open Air and sign in with your JetBrains Account.
Go to Settings | VCS Providers and connect GitHub. There’s no separate Copilot sign-in: Air uses this connection to sign in to GitHub Copilot on the cloud machine when the task starts.
Click New Task and pick a repository and a branch. Cloud agents work from a remote branch, so push your changes first.
Choose GitHub Copilot in the agent picker. If it isn’t there, ensure that GitHub is connected and that your GitHub account has a Copilot subscription. If the issue persists, get in touch with your Air admin.
Describe the task and click Send.
From your IDE
In your IDE, open Air, start a new task, and choose Cloud as the environment.
Pick a GitHub repository and a branch. Cloud agents work from a remote branch, so push your changes first. If GitHub isn’t connected yet, Air shows a banner asking you to authorize it.
Click Authorize and approve the GitHub app in your browser. The connection page doesn’t mention GitHub Copilot, but Air uses the same connection to sign in to both.
Your browser opens Settings | VCS Providers in the web version of Air, with GitHub connected.
Go back to your IDE and choose GitHub Copilot in the agent picker.
Describe the task and click Send.
After you send the task
The task shows up in the Tasks list under your repository, both in your IDE and on the web. GitHub Copilot starts in a fresh cloud machine. When it’s done, open the task and review its changes.
Where cloud tasks run
Each task gets its own virtual machine. GitHub Copilot runs in a Docker container, signed in to GitHub with your account. All its traffic goes through a proxy, and nothing carries over to the next task. So it can build, test, and install packages without touching your laptop. For more details, check out our blog post How Air Cloud-Based Agent Sandboxing Works in Air.
Run GitHub Copilot on a schedule or on every pull request
Automations start cloud tasks for you – either on a schedule or when something happens in your repository, such as a new pull request. If you pick GitHub Copilot as the agent, each run uses your Copilot plan.
We recommend starting with a weekly dependency update as your first automation: It’s easy to review and keeps credit usage predictable. In contrast, an automation that reviews every pull request can drain your credits much faster, especially if the repository is busy. Keep in mind that Air doesn’t warn you when your credits are all used up – your runs will just start failing.
FAQ
How is GitHub Copilot different from the other agents in Air?
GitHub, not Air, handles your Copilot account. When a task starts, the Copilot CLI checks your plan and credits with GitHub. Because Air doesn’t show your Copilot usage and can’t limit it, you have to keep track of it on GitHub.
Which GitHub Copilot plans can I use?
Any plan that GitHub accepts for the Copilot CLI. Air doesn’t check which specific plan you’re using.
Why did my task fail soon after it started?
Most likely, your GitHub plan has no credits left. Air checks that you have an active Copilot subscription before it starts a task, but it can’t see how many credits you have left. Check your usage on GitHub.
How do I know how many credits were spent on a task?
Check your usage on GitHub. Air doesn’t track Copilot credits for local or cloud tasks, and it can’t set a spending limit.

posts.title: Hear What Your IDE Is Doing: New Sound Cues in JetBrains IDEs
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
You can use the audio player below to listen to this blog post.

With JetBrains IDEs 2026.3, we’re adding a new way to stay connected to your work: sound cues.
A short sound can tell you if a build has finished successfully or failed, a breakpoint has been hit, or there’s something at the caret that needs your attention. These cues are designed to make everyday development easier to follow, whether you are concentrating on another task, working across several projects, or using a screen reader.
Sound is on by default for screen reader users, and opt-in otherwise. In both cases, the sound cues are configurable – you can choose the cues that help you and leave the rest off.
What you can hear
The new Sound Signals settings let your IDE provide audio feedback for all important events.
A video illustrating a sound signal for a failed test, as well as a sound for a breakpoint being hit. 



For long-running work, you can hear when a build, test, or other task finishes, with different cues for success, warnings, and errors. The IDE also plays a sound when a breakpoint is hit and while a background task is running, so you know where the progress is at without having to repeatedly check a status area.
Sound cues also cover editor line marks. When screen reader support is enabled, the IDE plays distinct cues as the caret reaches a line with:
An error 
A warning
A breakpoint
A version-control change
Folded code
These editor marks are usually communicated visually. The new cues provide an additional way to notice them while moving through code.
You can also enable sound for individual notification groups. For example, if a particular tool or workflow sends notifications you care about, you can choose to have the IDE play a sound for it.
Sounds for Air
JetBrains IDEs 2026.3 also ship with Air. Agent work can have the same rhythm as a long build: you set it in motion, then turn to another task or window while it works.
Air has four sound cues: one when the agent completes its work, one when it stops with an error, one when it needs your input, and one for starting and stopping dictation. The sounds for AI operations are distinct enough from general IDE sound cues for you to easily tell them apart. 
Air sounds can be configured separately in the dedicated settings section Settings | Tools | Air.
Choose the setup that works for you
IDE sound cues live on a new settings page built for accessibility. Settings | Appearance & Behavior | Accessibility now brings together Support screen readers, Zoom, contrast scrollbars, colors for red-green vision deficiency, the option to announce notifications with a screen reader, and sound cues, all in one place.
The new Accessibility page in the Settings with configurable options for Sound Signals in JetBrains IDEs.



If you use a screen reader, the relevant sound cues are enabled automatically when the Support screen readers option is on. This includes sound cues for IDE events (builds, tests, progress, and breakpoints) and editor line marks.
If you do not use a screen reader, sound cues are off by default. To enable them:
Open Settings/Preferences.
Go to Appearance & Behavior | Accessibility.
Find the Sound Signals section.
Turn on the sounds you would like to use.
You can preview each sound on the same page before enabling it, and turn off any cue that does not fit your workflow.
For a specific notification, go to Appearance & Behavior | Notifications, select the notification group in the list, and enable the Play sound option.
To learn more about configuring sound cues in your IDE, see this section in our accessibility documentation.
A note for VoiceOver users on macOS
By default, VoiceOver makes other sounds quieter while it speaks. If the IDE sounds are hard to hear, turn off audio ducking in the VoiceOver settings on your Mac.
A small cue can make a real difference
Development often involves waiting: for a test suite, a build, a background task, a debugger, or an agent to reach the right point. Sound cues let the IDE share that status in a lightweight way, so you can stay focused on the work in front of you.
For visually impaired developers, these sounds also make information available that was previously represented only on screen. Sound cues began with an accessibility request, and they are part of our ongoing work to make JetBrains IDEs more accessible rather than a one-off feature.
If you’d like to stay informed about accessibility improvements, you can subscribe to our accessibility updates here.
We’d love to hear from you
Sound cues will be available starting with the 2026.3 release of JetBrains IDEs, but you can already try them out in our Release Candidate builds. 
We’re eager to hear from developers who rely on accessibility features, as well as from anyone interested in improving the experience of using them. If you have ideas or feedback about accessibility in JetBrains IDEs, you can reach us directly at accessibility@jetbrains.com. You can also report issues through YouTrack or the support request form.

posts.title: The eMudhra Certificate Authority Compromise: What It Means for TeamCity
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Summary
In October 2026, the private keys of eight intermediate certificate authorities operated by eMudhra were found to be weak and recoverable from public data. According to eMudhra’s official statement, none of the affected intermediate CAs had issued end-entity (leaf) certificates, and eMudhra is not aware of evidence that the weak keys were recovered or exploited before the issue was disclosed.
The issue is not a vulnerability in TeamCity itself. However, the trust stores maintained by other software components (primarily the Java runtime) that TeamCity relies on may continue to trust the compromised certificates. Starting with versions 2026.2.2 and 2026.1.6, TeamCity shows a health report if the installation still trusts affected certificates, along with remediation steps.
Recommended actions:
TeamCity On-Premises: Review server and build agent installations and apply the necessary fixes according to the instructions below. Upgrade to v2026.2.2 or v2026.1.6 for an updated Java runtime for the Windows agent installer, updated Docker images, and the health report, or follow the instructions below to apply the same fixes to the current installation.
TeamCity Cloud: TeamCity Cloud has already been updated. Certificates uploaded to TeamCity must be reviewed as described in Certificates uploaded to TeamCity below. Self-hosted build agents must also be reviewed according to the instructions below.
Details
On October 17, 2026, the private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CAs, six for TLS and two for code signing, were reported as compromised. This is an industry-wide certificate authority incident, not an issue specific to TeamCity. Certificates issued with these keys would look valid to any software that still trusts them.
Browser and OS vendors have released updates that block the compromised certificates, and systems are protected once they install them. Software with its own trust store, such as a Java runtime, keeps trusting the compromised certificates until that trust store is updated. TeamCity’s server and build agents use the trust store of their Java runtime.
TeamCity downloads are not signed by an eMudhra CA and are not affected.
What you need to do
1. Update the Java runtime
Identify the Java runtime used by each server node and agent, including any custom trust store set with javax.net.ssl.trustStore.
Check the Java vendor’s release notes for CVE-2026-91403 and CVE-2026-114820. For Amazon Corretto 21, the fixed build is 21.0.13.0.11 or later.
Update affected runtimes and restart each server node or agent.
Optional trust-store verification can identify affected certificates still present in a trust store. If upgrading is not feasible, follow the manual mitigation commands in the same section.
Removing AAA Certificate Services can disrupt unaffected services; test dependent connections before removing that root.
2. Update your TeamCity server and review uploaded certificates
The following server maintenance recommendations apply to TeamCity On-Premises installations. JetBrains patches TeamCity Cloud, but certificates uploaded to the service still require review.
Upgrade TeamCity if possible. Releases 2026.2.2 and 2026.1.6 add the health report, other product improvements, and fixes for other vulnerabilities. Existing agents require an independent review.
Update Java on every server node. Follow Update the Java runtime, even after upgrading TeamCity.
Redeploy Docker installations. Pull the patched 2026.2.2 or 2026.1.6 server image from Docker Hub once published, or rebuild the existing image using the server image instructions. Recreate the containers.
Review uploaded certificates. Use the health report or the certificate inspection commands below and then remove affected certificates through the Root project’s SSL / HTTPS Certificates page. Updating Java does not remove uploaded certificates.
Updating the TeamCity server does not update integrations or third-party software. Review those components separately as described in Review and update supporting infrastructure.
3. Update your TeamCity agents and review trusted certificates
Update Java on every build agent. Follow Update the Java runtime. TeamCity Cloud customers must also review the Java runtimes used by their self-hosted agents. The health report does not check agents.
Update Docker installations. Pull the patched 2026.2.2 or 2026.1.6 agent image from Docker Hub. Alternatively, rebuild the existing image using the same rebuild instructions as for the server image. Recreate the containers using the updated image.
Review agent certificates. Run the certificate inspection commands under Technical commands from <agent home>/conf/trustedCertificates and remove any affected certificate files. Updating Java does not remove these certificates.
4. Review and update supporting infrastructure
Updating the server does not update integrations or third-party software. We recommend reviewing these components independently:
Operating systems and build tools: Apply vendor updates to OS trust stores, other Java runtimes, Git and MinGit, Python’s certifi, Node.js, and other tools with separate trust stores.
Custom images: Update the OS and tools inside each affected image, rebuild the image, and recreate the containers.
Connected services: Replace eMudhra certificates used by VCS hosts, package registries, and other services through eMudhra’s migration process.
5. Update TeamCity CLI
TeamCity CLI is distributed separately from the server and agents and requires its own update. Version 1.6.1 (October 26, 2026) was rebuilt with Go 1.27.3, which includes the fix.
Run teamcity update on every machine where the CLI is used, including build agents, and confirm the version with teamcity --version. Other installation methods are listed on the release page.
Technical commands
Each script defines its environment variables at the top:
TEAMCITY_JRE: Defaults to JAVA_HOME; change it if TeamCity runs on another JRE or JDK.
TC_TRUSTSTORE: Set to any custom javax.net.ssl.trustStore (JDK 8 default: jre/lib/security/cacerts).
TC_STOREPASS: Change it if the password differs.
TC_CERT_DIR: The certificate file to inspect, where indicated.
Optional trust-store verification
Please note the result applies only to the selected trust store. The commands do not inspect blocked.certs.
Linux and macOS (Bash or zsh):
(
export TEAMCITY_JRE="${TEAMCITY_JRE:-$JAVA_HOME}"
export TC_TRUSTSTORE="$TEAMCITY_JRE/lib/security/cacerts"
export TC_STOREPASS='changeit'

keytool="${TEAMCITY_JRE:?Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use}/bin/keytool"
[ -x "$keytool" ] || { echo "ERROR: keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin/ and lib/)." >&2; exit 1; }
output=$("$keytool" -J-Duser.language=en -list -v \
  -keystore "$TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS) ||
  { echo "ERROR: Certificate check failed." >&2; printf '%s\n' "$output" >&2; exit 1; }

awk '
  /^Alias name:/ { alias=$0 }
  /86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6|CN=EM (DV|OV|EV) (TLS|CS) CA - G3/ {
    found=1; print alias; print
  }
  END {
    print found ? "ACTION REQUIRED: this trust store still trusts compromised eMudhra certificates (listed above). Update the Java runtime or apply the manual mitigation." \
                : "OK: no compromised eMudhra certificates found in this trust store. No action is needed for it."
  }
' <<< "$output"
)
Windows (PowerShell):
& {
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { $env:TEAMCITY_JRE = $env:JAVA_HOME }
$env:TC_TRUSTSTORE = "$env:TEAMCITY_JRE\lib\security\cacerts"
$env:TC_STOREPASS = 'changeit'

if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { throw 'Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use.' }
$keytool = "$env:TEAMCITY_JRE\bin\keytool.exe"
if (-not [IO.File]::Exists($keytool)) { throw "keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin\ and lib\)." }
$prev = $ErrorActionPreference; $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
$output = & $keytool '-J-Duser.language=en' -list -v -keystore "$env:TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS 2>&1
$ErrorActionPreference = $prev
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "ERROR: Certificate check failed. $output" }

$pattern = '86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6|CN=EM (DV|OV|EV) (TLS|CS) CA - G3'
$alias = ''
$found = $false
foreach ($line in $output) {
    if ($line -match '^Alias name:') { $alias = $line }
    if ($line -match $pattern) { $found = $true; $alias; $line }
}
if ($found) { 'ACTION REQUIRED: this trust store still trusts compromised eMudhra certificates (listed above). Update the Java runtime or apply the manual mitigation.' }
else { 'OK: no compromised eMudhra certificates found in this trust store. No action is needed for it.' }
}
Certificates uploaded to TeamCity
The health report in versions 2026.2.2 and 2026.1.6 lists affected server certificates. For manual inspection, check custom certificates and identify the affected ones.
Set path to the directory with custom certificates (TC_CERT_DIR) to the following and run the command:
Server: <TeamCity Data Directory>/config/projects/_Root/pluginData/trustedCertificates
Agent: <agent home>/conf/trustedCertificates




Linux and macOS (Bash or zsh):
(
export TEAMCITY_JRE="${TEAMCITY_JRE:-$JAVA_HOME}"
export TC_CERT_DIR="${TC_CERT_DIR:-/path/to/trusted/certificates}"

keytool="${TEAMCITY_JRE:?Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use}/bin/keytool"
[ -x "$keytool" ] || { echo "ERROR: keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin/ and lib/)." >&2; exit 1; }
[ -d "$TC_CERT_DIR" ] || { echo "ERROR: directory not found: $TC_CERT_DIR. Either no custom certificates have been added yet (TeamCity creates the directory on the first upload), or TC_CERT_DIR is incorrect (server: <TeamCity Data Directory>/config/projects/_Root/pluginData/trustedCertificates, agent: <agent home>/conf/trustedCertificates)." >&2; exit 1; }
found=0
while IFS= read -r f; do
  output=$("$keytool" -J-Duser.language=en -printcert -v -file "$f") ||
    { echo "ERROR: Cannot read $f." >&2; printf '%s\n' "$output" >&2; exit 1; }
  if grep -Eq '86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6|CN=EM (DV|OV|EV) (TLS|CS) CA - G3' <<< "$output"; then
    echo "AFFECTED: $f"; found=1
  fi
done < <(find "$TC_CERT_DIR" -maxdepth 1 -type f)
[ "$found" = 1 ] && echo "ACTION REQUIRED: the files listed above are compromised eMudhra certificates. Remove them (server: SSL/HTTPS Certificates page; agent: delete the files)." ||
  echo "OK: no compromised eMudhra certificates found in $TC_CERT_DIR. No action is needed."
)
Windows (PowerShell):
& {
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { $env:TEAMCITY_JRE = $env:JAVA_HOME }
if (-not $env:TC_CERT_DIR) { $env:TC_CERT_DIR = 'C:\path\to\trusted\certificates' }

if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { throw 'Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use.' }
$keytool = "$env:TEAMCITY_JRE\bin\keytool.exe"
if (-not [IO.File]::Exists($keytool)) { throw "keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin\ and lib\)." }
if (-not [IO.Directory]::Exists($env:TC_CERT_DIR)) { throw "ERROR: directory not found: $env:TC_CERT_DIR. Either no custom certificates have been added yet (TeamCity creates the directory on the first upload), or TC_CERT_DIR is incorrect (server: <TeamCity Data Directory>\config\projects\_Root\pluginData\trustedCertificates, agent: <agent home>\conf\trustedCertificates)." }
$pattern = '86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6|CN=EM (DV|OV|EV) (TLS|CS) CA - G3'
$found = $false
foreach ($file in Get-ChildItem -LiteralPath $env:TC_CERT_DIR -File) {
    $output = & $keytool '-J-Duser.language=en' -printcert -v -file $file.FullName
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "ERROR: Cannot read $($file.FullName). $output" }
    if ($output -match $pattern) { "AFFECTED: $($file.FullName)"; $found = $true }
}
if ($found) { 'ACTION REQUIRED: the files listed above are compromised eMudhra certificates. Remove them (server: SSL/HTTPS Certificates page; agent: delete the files).' }
else { "OK: no compromised eMudhra certificates found in $env:TC_CERT_DIR. No action is needed." }
}
Manual mitigation commands
Before execution, make sure TEAMCITY_JRE in the current terminal points to the runtime actually running the TeamCity component:
Server: Consult this configuration reference.
Agents: Check teamcity.agent.jvm.java.home on the agent’s Parameters tab, as described in the Java Update Guide.
Copy lib/security/blocked.certs from a JDK containing the fix for CVE-2026-91403 to the same location in the runtime in use. Java 8 uses jre/lib/security/blacklisted.certs, while some Java 11 and 13 builds also use blacklisted.certs, so verify the path before copying.
Back up the trust store. Removing AAA Certificate Services can disrupt unaffected services; test dependent connections first.
Run the command below. It uses the same script header as the verification commands above, finds the affected roots listed above by fingerprint, and deletes them. Running it again is safe.
Linux and macOS (Bash or zsh):
(
export TEAMCITY_JRE="${TEAMCITY_JRE:-$JAVA_HOME}"
export TC_TRUSTSTORE="$TEAMCITY_JRE/lib/security/cacerts"
export TC_STOREPASS='changeit'

keytool="${TEAMCITY_JRE:?Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use}/bin/keytool"
[ -x "$keytool" ] || { echo "ERROR: keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin/ and lib/)." >&2; exit 1; }
[ -w "$TC_TRUSTSTORE" ] || { echo "ERROR: cannot write to $TC_TRUSTSTORE (missing or no permission). Run with sudo or as the owner of the Java installation." >&2; exit 1; }
output=$("$keytool" -J-Duser.language=en -list -v \
  -keystore "$TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS) ||
  { echo "ERROR: Certificate check failed." >&2; printf '%s\n' "$output" >&2; exit 1; }

affected=$(awk '
  /^Alias name:/ { alias=substr($0, 13) }
  /SHA256: (86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D:3B:BE:27:34:C6:12:BA:34:1D:81:3E:04:3C:F9:E8:A8:62:CD:5C:57:A3:6B:BE:6B|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31:D7:71:E9:48:4E:BC:DE:F7:1D:5F:0C:3E:0A:29:48:78:2B:C8:3E:E0:EA:69:9E:F4|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A:83:DF:F9:AB:BB:A6:2E:DB:AF:6F:2D:10:2B:F2:57:FD:71:2F:4D:9F:27:46:ED:8D|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F:B4:D1:4C:9F:28:5F:8C:0B:AD:90:FC:3B:CC:1F:A0:7D:47:F4:71:8E:DA:BA:34:A5|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1:CD:1D:55:5A:4E:9C:CE:62:C7:F9:63:46:03:EE:40:66:15:83:3D:C8:C8:D0:03:67|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6:E3:B5:12:9A:00:BA:41:F7:EE:EF:02:08:72:F1:E6:50:4B:F0:F6:C3:F2:4F:3A:F3)/ { print alias }
' <<< "$output")
[ -n "$affected" ] || { echo "OK: this trust store contains no compromised eMudhra roots. Nothing to delete."; exit 0; }

while IFS= read -r alias; do
  echo "Deleting: $alias"
  "$keytool" -delete -alias "$alias" -keystore "$TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS || exit 1
done <<< "$affected"
echo "DONE: removed the compromised root certificates listed above. Restart the TeamCity server node or agent, then run the verification again."
)
Windows (PowerShell):
& {
$ErrorActionPreference = 'Stop'
if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { $env:TEAMCITY_JRE = $env:JAVA_HOME }
$env:TC_TRUSTSTORE = "$env:TEAMCITY_JRE\lib\security\cacerts"
$env:TC_STOREPASS = 'changeit'

if (-not $env:TEAMCITY_JRE) { throw 'Set TEAMCITY_JRE or JAVA_HOME to the Java home directory of the runtime in use.' }
$keytool = "$env:TEAMCITY_JRE\bin\keytool.exe"
if (-not [IO.File]::Exists($keytool)) { throw "keytool not found at $keytool. TEAMCITY_JRE must be the Java home directory (the folder that contains bin\ and lib\)." }
try { [IO.File]::Open($env:TC_TRUSTSTORE, 'Open', 'ReadWrite').Dispose() }
catch { throw "ERROR: cannot write to $env:TC_TRUSTSTORE. Run PowerShell as Administrator or as the owner of the Java installation. ($($_.Exception.Message))" }
$prev = $ErrorActionPreference; $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
$output = & $keytool '-J-Duser.language=en' -list -v -keystore "$env:TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS 2>&1
$ErrorActionPreference = $prev
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "ERROR: Certificate check failed. $output" }

$roots = '86:A1:EC:BA:08:9C:4A:8D:3B:BE:27:34:C6:12:BA:34:1D:81:3E:04:3C:F9:E8:A8:62:CD:5C:57:A3:6B:BE:6B|D7:A7:A0:FB:5D:7E:27:31:D7:71:E9:48:4E:BC:DE:F7:1D:5F:0C:3E:0A:29:48:78:2B:C8:3E:E0:EA:69:9E:F4|7D:D7:8D:5F:4F:13:45:9A:83:DF:F9:AB:BB:A6:2E:DB:AF:6F:2D:10:2B:F2:57:FD:71:2F:4D:9F:27:46:ED:8D|F2:ED:AA:FF:3D:9B:70:1F:B4:D1:4C:9F:28:5F:8C:0B:AD:90:FC:3B:CC:1F:A0:7D:47:F4:71:8E:DA:BA:34:A5|40:F6:AF:03:46:A9:9A:A1:CD:1D:55:5A:4E:9C:CE:62:C7:F9:63:46:03:EE:40:66:15:83:3D:C8:C8:D0:03:67|1A:A0:C2:70:9E:83:1B:D6:E3:B5:12:9A:00:BA:41:F7:EE:EF:02:08:72:F1:E6:50:4B:F0:F6:C3:F2:4F:3A:F3'
$alias = ''
$aliases = foreach ($line in $output) {
    if ($line -match '^Alias name: (.+)$') { $alias = $Matches[1] }
    if ($line -match "SHA256: ($roots)") { $alias }
}
if (-not $aliases) { 'OK: this trust store contains no compromised eMudhra roots. Nothing to delete.'; return }

foreach ($a in $aliases) {
    "Deleting: $a"
    $ErrorActionPreference = 'Continue'
    $result = & $keytool -delete -alias $a -keystore "$env:TC_TRUSTSTORE" -storepass:env TC_STOREPASS 2>&1
    $ErrorActionPreference = $prev
    if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw "ERROR: Failed to delete $a. $result" }
}
'DONE: removed the compromised root certificates listed above. Restart the TeamCity server node or agent, then run the verification again.'
}
Afterwards, run the verification commands above to confirm the roots are gone. Restart the server node or agent after completing the mitigation. Include any custom trust stores in the review.
Security Bulletin
JetBrains’ assessment and guidance on the eMudhra Certificate Authority incident is available here.
Frequently asked questions
Is TeamCity affected?
Not directly. As a CI/CD system, TeamCity connects to multiple integrations and relies on Java runtimes, build tools, and other components with separate trust stores. These trust stores require independent review and updates, as described in What you need to do.
Do I need to upgrade?
Upgrading to 2026.2.2 or 2026.1.6 is recommended. These releases add the health report, other product improvements, and fixes for other vulnerabilities.
Upgrading TeamCity does not always update Java, so review the corresponding runtime using the Optional trust-store verification section above. If upgrading TeamCity is not currently an option, apply the mitigations described in If upgrading is not feasible above.
Is TeamCity Cloud affected?
TeamCity Cloud has already been updated, but customers must still check:
Self-hosted agents using TeamCity Agents, as described above.
Certificates uploaded to TeamCity, as described above.
Does the health report check build agents?
No. The health report checks the server nodes only. Check and fix build agents manually, as described in TeamCity Agents above.
Which TeamCity Docker images are affected?
Images for versions 2026.2.2 and 2026.1.6 are patched, so please update if possible. Older images can be patched as described in TeamCity Server and TeamCity Agents above, and then used to recreate the containers.
Is TeamCity CLI affected?
Yes. TeamCity CLI is a Go application, and versions before 1.6.1 were built with an affected Go release. Update as described in Update TeamCity CLI.
Support
For any questions regarding this issue, please get in touch with the TeamCity Support team by submitting a ticket. To report a security issue in TeamCity, please follow our Coordinated Disclosure Policy.
